notes.b: Everyone knows what a family is, but defining it exactly is harder than it looks. The core idea is kinship, meaning the ties of blood, marriage or adoption that link people.
points: A family is a group of people related by blood (birth), marriage or adoption, and it is the basic social unit of society. It supports its members and passes values from one generation to the next.
Traditional definition: a group related by blood, marriage or adoption, usually living together and sharing responsibility for its members.
Kinship is the tie that makes a group a family: the links of blood, marriage or adoption, or common ancestry (lineage).

George Peter Murdock (Social Structure, 1949) defined the family as a social group with common residence, economic co-operation and reproduction. This is one classic sociological definition among several, and later sociologists criticise it as too narrow.
Article 41 of the Constitution of Ireland (1937) describes the family as the natural, primary and fundamental unit group of society, and protects it.
Article 41.3 pledges to guard the institution of marriage on which the family is founded, so the protection has traditionally been for the family founded on marriage.

A household is people living at the same address and sharing living arrangements. A family can span more than one household, for example when grandparents living elsewhere, a parent working abroad or separated parents remain part of the family group.
Not every household is a family, because a household may contain unrelated people.

Legal definitions are narrower and focus on marriage, blood and adoption ties, because they decide rights such as inheritance and maintenance. Sociological definitions focus on the relationships and functions of the group, so they can include cohabiting couples, lone parents and same-sex parents.
notes.tip: Start with the definition: related by blood, marriage or adoption, and the basic unit of society that supports its members and passes on values. Do not define the family only as a mother, father and children, because that is one structure (the nuclear family). The 2024 referendum proposal to change Article 41 was rejected, so do not say the Constitution was changed.

notes.h: Why one definition is not enough: comparing criteria
notes.b: No single definition fits every society or every household. Each criterion used in a definition leaves some real families out, so a good definition combines several.
points: A definition based only on marriage excludes cohabiting couples with children and lone-parent families, so sociologists usually include the parent-child relationship.
A definition based only on shared residence excludes family members who live apart, such as a parent working abroad.
A definition based only on blood excludes adoptive and step relationships, which is why adoption is included alongside blood and marriage.

Criteria used in most definitions: blood or adoptive ties, marriage or a committed partnership, shared residence, shared economic life (pooling income and sharing expenses), raising children, and mutual support and obligation.
You should be able to build a working definition by combining criteria, for example blood, marriage or adoption plus mutual support.
notes.tip: If asked for two criteria used in defining a family, name them and say which kind of family each would leave out.

notes.b: Universality means a family of some kind exists in every known human society, although its form (structure) differs from one society to another. It does not mean every society has the same kind of family.
points: Every known society has a family group that raises children and organises kinship relationships.
What is universal: kinship ties, the rearing of children, the care of dependants, and the passing on of values and culture.

What varies: size, structure (nuclear, extended, polygamous and matrilineal forms are all found in different cultures), who lives together, where couples live after marriage, how descent and inheritance are traced, and the roles of members.

The structure of a family is shaped by economic conditions (such as farming or industry), religion and culture, and law and political conditions, so one family type is not found everywhere and no one form is natural everywhere.
The functions of the family, such as raising children and caring for dependants, appear in all societies even where the structure differs.
notes.tip: Universality means every society has a family, not that every society has the same family. Give one sentence of explanation, such as an example of forms that vary, to secure full marks. Universality is not uniformity.

notes.h: Terms for marriage, descent and residence (assumed knowledge)
notes.b: Sociologists use a small set of terms to describe how families are organised in different societies. Each one answers a different question: how many partners, whose line, where the couple lives and how people are related.
points: Monogamy is marriage to one partner at a time; it does not mean one partner for life. Serial monogamy is a succession of single marriages or partnerships, one after another, such as remarriage after divorce.
Polygamy is marriage to more than one spouse at the same time. Polygyny is one husband with several wives, and polyandry is one wife with several husbands.

Patrilineal descent traces family and inheritance through the father's line; matrilineal descent traces them through the mother's line. Bilateral descent traces them through both, which is the pattern in Ireland.
Matrilineal is about descent and inheritance, not about who holds political power or who heads the household.

Patrilocal residence means a couple lives with or near the husband's family; matrilocal residence means they live with or near the wife's family. Neolocal residence means the couple sets up a new home of their own, the common modern pattern. These describe where a couple lives, not who inherits.
Consanguineal relatives are related by blood; affinal relatives are related by marriage (in-laws).
The family of orientation is the family you are born into; the family of procreation is the family you form.
notes.tip: Expect a term to be given and defined in one or two lines, for example monogamy, polygamy, serial monogamy, matrilineal or patrilocal. Do not confuse polygamy (more than one spouse) with polygyny (one husband, several wives) or polyandry (one wife, several husbands).

notes.b: Looking at families in other societies shows which features are found everywhere and which change from place to place. This comparison is the evidence for universality.
points: The Minangkabau of West Sumatra, Indonesia, are a matrilineal society in which descent is traced and family property is passed through the female line. This shows that a family can be organised around women's lines, though it does not mean women rule.

Kibbutzim in Israel historically raised children in communal children's houses, with parents visiting. This shows that some family functions can be carried out beyond the household, shared with the community while kinship remains. The practice has largely ended.
Other forms include polygamous families in societies where polygyny is accepted, extended households of several generations in many societies, and the nuclear family in industrial societies.

Comparing cases shows which features are universal, such as kinship and child rearing, and which vary, such as residence, descent and household size. The structure varies with the society, but a family group is always present.

You may be given a literature or film extract or a short description of a family in another society. Apply the terms to it by identifying the descent pattern, the residence and the form of marriage, and say what remains universal.
notes.tip: In a case-study question, identify the form (extended, polygamous or matrilineal) and then say what remains universal. Do not say the Minangkabau are ruled by women, and use the past tense for the kibbutz children's houses.

questions.prompt: Outline two ways in which the family may be defined.
questions.model: Two definitions, each with explanation. Traditional definition: a group related by blood, marriage or adoption who usually share responsibility for one another. Sociological definition: a social group with common residence, economic co-operation and reproduction (Murdock). Alternatively, the Article 41 description of the family as the natural, primary and fundamental unit group of society, with the reason it is described that way.

questions.prompt: Examine how the family is found in all known societies while its structure varies from one culture to another, giving examples.
questions.model: Universality: every known society has a family group that raises children and organises kinship. Variation: nuclear, extended, polygamous and matrilineal forms are found in different cultures. Explanation of variation: economic, religious and political conditions shape structure, e.g. patrilineal descent where inheritance passes through the father's line, matrilocal residence where the couple lives with the wife's family. Example case: the Minangkabau of West Sumatra with matrilineal property. Conclusion of the argument: the form varies but the basic functions and kinship ties remain in every society.
